title: San Francisco’s Homekey buildings: State grant, City price and the tax roll
question: For each San Francisco Homekey award since Round 2, which building and parcel is it, what did the City pay, how does the grant compare with the State’s caps and with awards elsewhere, and what does the roll show?
finding: 9 awards, $236,844,933 for 718 homes; 8 tie to a Board acceptance file by the exact sum and 7 to a City purchase. All 4 Round 2 grants are within the notice’s caps (0 above): capital per home $230,531 to $289,312 against at most $300,000. 1321 Mission (1321 Mission Street): price $86,500,000, $540,625 a home, 1.29 times the 2021-22 roll value; Eula Hotel Apartments (3055-3061 16th Street): price $5,600,000, $224,000 a home, 2.6 times the 2021-22 roll value; Mission Inn (5630 Mission Street): price $17,000,000, $333,333 a home, 1.33 times the 2021-22 roll value; City Gardens (333-12th Street): price $145,000,000, $852,941 a home, 2.79 times the 2020-21 roll value. The Board accepted $7,480,080, not the $7,194,080 on the State's list; the Budget and Legislative Analyst's report on this file names the Eula Hotel.
how: San Francisco rows of the State’s Round 2, Round 3 and Homekey+ lists (the Round 2 list saved by the owner is byte-identical to the copy already on disk). Each is tied to the Board file that accepted the grant by the exact award sum in the file title; a purchase file is the passed Board file that buys the same street number and street. Parcels are those the parcels screen matched to that purchase file. The roll value before is land plus improvements on the last roll (portal or workbook) of the purchase year or earlier with a value. Caps are read from the Round 2 notice (Sections 205 to 207).
limits: Homes are the units on the State list, which can be fewer than the rooms bought when a hotel is converted (the notice counts doors at acquisition), so the price per home can overstate. Homekey awards are what the State granted, not what a building cost; the City adds money and nonprofits may own the building. Rounds 3 and Homekey+ had their own notices, which are not on disk, so their caps are not checked. A building that has not sold for years usually sells above its roll value (the roll moves at most 2% a year without a sale). Being within the caps says nothing about whether the price was right; the appraisal the notice requires would. Round 2 money went first come, first served to applications that met the threshold, including a minimum of 120 points (Sections 304 and 400); the State’s racial-equity analysis is one scoring category worth up to 10 points, a policy requirement about the applicant’s plan, and no application’s score is published, so the order of awards cannot be tested. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
